Time to go sailing.

So I never spent anytime on the water....ever.... I had no idea how the water worked. Ended up living and working in a city (seattle) that maybe is one of the best sailing cities int he world, but never realized it for years.

Then one day, saw a sailboat race going out on Lake Union , which is a large lake almost right in the center of the city, it looked cool and was different and decided to give sailing a try.

Ended up becoming "rail meat" in the local racing fleet by posting an ad on CL and hooked up with a few of the racing crews (sailors are generally a fairly open culture and almost any sail boat would love to have you along as crew.) and ended up on "crazy Capt Mikes" boat.

Cpt Mike was a bit of a character,(to say the least) but was a absolute master sailor and I ended up crewing and learning how to sail on his boat for two years. Sailed three-four times a week and fell in love with it and did all the races we could. (and we were always in the top three boats in any race. We were a FAST boat, after we got the crew jelled, in the top ten fastest in the entire Puget sound anyway...)

Side note: Racing is where you really learn to sail and sail fast. Sailing fast is the key for cruising long distance, so you can actually get there. So start figuring out how to get on a race boat somewhere and crew. There are lots of low ball and "drink and race" type races anyplace that there are more then about three sailboats....

Anyway, CPT MIke was also a "cruiser" and would take off solo for weeks at a time sometimes on the boat and sail all over and I got hooked on the idea of having a fully self contained environment (a sailboat) that could travel anywhere...

After two years crewing on his boat, I felt I knew enough to run my own boat and bought a $800.00 Coronado 24 of off CL. It was a RAT boat. Real run down... but I loved her. (There's no love, like your first) But it also forced me to learn how to refurb and repair all the systems on a sailboat.

After a year sailing her in the sound, I spent a summer (4 months) and sailed her solo up and back the inside passage.

Best thing I have ever done. I am currently planning on getting a bigger boat and doing the pirate run in the Bahamas for 9 months or so. Cuz....why not.

So that all being said. Here's what I would suggest.

Start sailing as a crew on many different boats. This will give you a great exposure to different types of boats and captains and you'll pick up a huge amount of skills you will need. (also you may find you really don't like sailing) Place an ad on CL that you want to crew and you'll be on your first boat withing days. Be cool and easy going and bring some wine or chocolate enough for the crew when you go and you'll be welcome an any boat.

Not all boats are worth staying on though. Some captains are wankers and some run a unsafe boat, some are raging drunks and some aren't that fun.... Your gut will tell you, if it doesn't, you should rethink being a captain of a boat if your instincts aren't any good. The ocean can be a VERY harsh mistress....

If you can' crew on a boat t(or even if you can) buy a small sailing dinghy and start sailing. 500 bucks gets you a a 2 man laser or a international 470. that can be thrown in the back of a truck or towed behind a small car. Sail the shit out of it. You'll only learn if you do it and the sailing principles you will learn are the exact same on a small 2 man race dinghy or a 50 foot J boat.

Read, read every book you can on sailing. You'll glean a huge amount of info you'll eventually need.

DON"T sell your house. You always need a base of operations. I lived on my sailboat for a year and was VERY ready to move back into a house afterwards. Plus having a backup is nice in case something goes wrong somewhere and you sink the boat or get injured or some such thing. you always have a house to go back to.

Save. Start saving money. The old adage: "Boats are really nothing more then holes in the water you throw money in" is apt. Although I never seemed to have to spend the insane amounts of money that everyone else does. But you are going to need money to cruise around the world. Sailboats are SUPER cheap to run (no fuel used really, which is maybe the biggest expense of running a boat) but you will always need repairs, dock fees, insurance, food.ect...

Start now on building out a business that you can do from the boat. Design mobile apps, blog, remote contracting. whatever. but start now, so you have your business all built up BEFORE you leave.

Also, respect the water. The ocean can be a very dangerous place and things can go from super smooth to insane crazy in just moments. It's like nothing you'll ever experience on land...ever (except maybe war)

Don't plan on sailing around the world for years but plan on working up into long distant runs. The west coast to Hawaii. Sail around the Florida keys... Sail the Bahamas. Sail from east coast to the Med and then up the canals of Europe. Do the Baja -Haha (Annual run down the west coast to Panama for the winters)

Do it. Just do it. Millions and millions of men and woman have done it before you and "what one man can do, another can do...." Life is WAY to short. and sailing is just very..... satiating. You will learn things about yourself and the world around you that you would never have an opportunity to learn anyway else....
